utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I'd like to briefly deal with some -- with a follow-up on documents which were tendered through Witness Barry Hogan. The Chamber would like to address some pending issues with respect to the materials tendered through Witness Barry Hogan on the 1st of October of this year. In relation to D381, the exhibit numbers reserved for extracts of the video bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1D1310 and 22311F, the Chamber recalls that it invited the parties to agree on which portions of this video, and any related testimonial material from a previous case, should be received into evidence. You can find this on transcript pages 17743 to 17748. The Chamber has yet to be informed of any such agreement. In relation to D382, the exhibit number reserved for the video bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D1312, the Chamber notes that this video was marked for identification, pending provision of the extract by the Defence. This can be found at transcript pages 17756 to 57. Or perhaps I should read it in full. That is, 17757. The Chamber was provided with a DVD containing the video on the 7th of November and therefore admitted D382 into evidence. With regard to D384 and D385, exhibit numbers reserved for other portions of the larger video bearing ERN V000-3497-1-A, the Chamber recalls that it asked the parties to agree on which portions of the video should be received as evidence and the best means of doing so. This can be found at transcript pages 17760 and 17767 to 17768. The Chamber notes that on the 7th of November, 2013, it received a DVD from the Defence containing a video bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D1312A, however, it has not received any indication from the parties with respect to an agreement on this matter. Additionally, with regard to Rule 65 ter number 19792, the Chamber notes the parties indicated that they would agree on which portions of the photographs should be admitted. This can be found at transcript pages 17774 to 17776. Similarly, the Chamber has yet to be informed of any agreement on the matter. The Chamber again invites the parties to provide, by the 22nd of November, updates on these matters, as well as make available any corresponding videos or photographs the parties wish to be admitted. Finally, given that transcript pages 17781 to 17782 are unclear with respect to the admission of P2430, the Chamber clarifies for the record that P2430 was admitted into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's comments on the matter, and invites the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kalbarczyk, I presume. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is handed out to you. I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Kalbarczyk. Is the Prosecution ready to start its examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, you'll first be examined by Ms. MacGregor. You'll find her to your right and she is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you please first state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Janusz Kalbarczyk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: According to your statement, you were a member of the Polish air force. Can you please provide the year of retirement and the rank that you retired at.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I left the armed forces in 1996. That was in September. I was then a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Is it correct that in April 1995 you were seconded from the Polish air force to the UN to serve in Bosnia as a Military Observer?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, this is true. This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you testify about that experience at this Tribunal in the Karadzic trial?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I testified against -- in the case against Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review parts of that testimony before today?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity, and it helped me a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Was that testimony true, to the best of your knowledge, when you gave it?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, it was true to my best knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you were today asked the same answers -- excuse me, the same questions, would you give the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Let's try. I don't really know what the questions are going to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My question is: If today I asked you the exact same questions that you were asked in Karadzic, do you believe that you would provide the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I hope I would. If the memory doesn't fail me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer to please show 65 ter 30456. This is the witness's ICTI witness statement -- ICTY. And please show page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: There's a document that will come to your screen shortly. And I ask you if you recognise that document, once you see it.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement. It has been signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review the statement prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to review the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer to please show page 4 in both the English and the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, I'm going to bring your attention to the statement where it refers to the second day of your imprisonment. In the penultimate paragraph of this page, and it starts with the phrase "at about 11.00," the final sentence of that paragraph says that were not interviewed. Were you, in fact, interviewed on the second day of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. It is difficult to say it was an interview. It was my statement, a very short statement, about what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you were asked the same -- about the same -- about the substance of these matters again, would you give the same answers that are contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And having taken the solemn oath today, do you affirm that the information in this document, along with the change we've just discussed, is accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, they are truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 30456. I also tender excerpts from the witness's Karadzic testimony which has been assigned 65 ter 30457.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't hear anything, Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kalbarczyk, you said twice that you would probably give the same answers. Is it your recollection that the answers were truthful and that's the reason why you think you would give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the same meaning word for word. I used the word "probably" because I would be referring to the same, same meaning, but I don't know whether I would be using exactly the same words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Madam Registrar. Thank you, Mr. Kalbarczyk.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30456 receives number P2801. And document 30457 receives number P2802, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2801 and P2802 -- yes, I'm sorry I misspoke, although I'm corrected by the transcriber which is okay. So, therefore, P2801 and P2802 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I please read a brief summary of the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Janusz Kalbarczyk was a Polish United Nations Military Observer who was deployed to Pale in April 1995. Mr. Kalbarczyk was taken hostage on 26 May 1995 and, along with other UNMOs, was threatened with death and used as a human shield by VRS forces. The witness was released on 13 June 1995. If I may continue with some questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any additional questions, you may put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have a few brief questions, sir, about your background as an UNMO. Within your UN contingent - not within the Polish air force - what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I was then colonel. I was deputy commander of the air force school in the Polish armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And within the UN contingent, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I was then major.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What were your duties as a UN Military Observer in Pale?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: As a UN -- UNMO, I was subordinated to the Sarajevo Sector. There were a few teams deployed on the Bosnian Serbs aside and also on the side of the opponents, Muslims. My main duty was to control the observance of the truce, armistice, that was signed by both sides, also to follow any changes that could have taken place in the territory in the area that we were asked to supervise and also to report to the sector about any alarming changes, movements of the armies that we have noticed or any use of arms or weapons, which should not have been used. Most generally -- and also being on duty on the radio in order to have -- to be in contact with the command of the sector, reporting on all major events that could have happened in the territory that we patrolled. The main job was to be part of the patrol unit. There were usually two observers on the patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kalbarczyk. I notice that the translation that came through, and this is at line 17 of page 7, it says in the English: "My main duty was to control" basically the armistice. Did you say "to control" or "to patrol"?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Supervising, patrolling, whether this armistice that was signed was -- was observed. We had a right to -- to -- to check the combat check-points of the army, Serbian army, where they had their cannons, for example, where there was a group of soldiers who stayed there 24 hours per day. We were allowed to check whether the weapons have not been used, whether there were not more people than the armistice provided for. So that was the -- that was our duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you've said that there were teams deployed both on the Bosnian Serb side and also on the Bosnian Muslim side. Which side were you deployed on while you were in Pale?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I was on the Bosnian -- Bosnian Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And were you armed as an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No. All observers, Military Observers, never carried any arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: A quick clarification. In your statement, you refer to Serb forces as the BSA. What does that abbreviation mean?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbian Army, as far as I remember. This is how I remembered it. When I was arrested, the -- the officer who -- who -- the officer -- this is the way that the officer introduced to us the soldiers who arrested us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you later come to hear another term to describe the Bosnian Serb forces, other than the BSA?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Not that I recall. No, I encountered no other terms. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, if there's any unclarity in the last paragraph of the first page, in substance, about the Vojska Republike Srpske, BSA, then please ask focussed questions on what might confuse, but until now it seems pretty clear to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Moving on to the events at the end of May 1995. In your statement, you describe that a police official with a pistol ordered you and the other UNMOs present to put your hands up. Did that official aim the pistol?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He put a pistol to my head. This official was very nervous. His hands were shaking. And he informed us that if the bombardments repeat, they have the order to shoot us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Moving on to the first location that you were taken to where you were in a ravine and handcuffed to a lightning rod. Did you later learn the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, afterwards. I didn't know for the first time what it was. I was there for the first time, ever. And then I learned that it was an area where we were prohibited from patrolling. We could not go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you ever learn the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: A colleague used the name Jahorinski Potok, and this is what I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the four to five hours that you were handcuffed to the lightning rod, can you estimate what the temperature was?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [In English] I don't have communication. [Interpretation] On that day, it was very, very hot. I think maybe around 26 to 27 degrees. No clouds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And can I check that you are now receiving the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can you hear the Polish interpretation of my questions?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I do -- yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, were you told what was going to happen to you next?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Never were we informed what will happen to us. Apart from the first day, when we were arrested, when the officer clearly stated that their task would be to kill us if the attack would be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: During the time that you were handcuffed to the lightning rod, what were you thinking about what would happen to you next?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I focussed on whether the attack would be repeated or not. Because if the air-strike was repeated, our chance of survival would be very small.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you told or did you understand why you were being handcuffed to the installation?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: At that time, it was not hard to guess that we were being used as human shields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, the Chamber wonders whether if the statement says it was very warm, whether we would have to know whether it was 26, 27 or 25 degrees. Similarly, the statement says: "Nobody explained to me why I was being handcuffed." Unless you think that the witness would depart from that statement, I wonder whether it should be asked again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It won't be asked again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'd actually like to now show the witness two video-clips, and, Your Honours, these are segments from the same video. The video has a 65 ter number 22417. This is a compilation of Bosnian Serb TV news broadcasts, and the two segments we have chosen are relevant to the witness's testimony. And if I can ask Ms. Stewart to show 22417B, the whole segment will be played, which is 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, if can you watch the video and at the end I will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The UNPROFOR members have -- the UNPROFOR members have also been positioned at other strategically important facilities that might be targets of NATO air-strikes. "[In English] From the air ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It is the international community and its decisions who have brought this situation upon these people. Whether they are going to survive depends on NATO actions."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I noticed that the substance of the interview was not translated. The full transcript has been uploaded into e-court into B/C/S and English. It's also been provided to the interpreters. I don't know if you want -- can rely on that in e-court or if you want it to be played again. I won't be asking any questions about the substance of the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the -- if the Prosecution does not rely on any of the words spoken, Mr. Stojanovic, would we need to play it twice or is it sufficient that we have looked at the images?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we re-play it once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll re-play it, and the interpreters can rely on the transcripts that were distributed. Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, we're going to play the clip again with translation -- excuse me, with interpretation of the bit of the interview, with the reporter speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can ask Ms. Stewart to again play the clip. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Reporter 1: The UNPROFOR members have also been positioned at other strategically important facilities that might be targets of NATO air-strikes. "Reporter 2: Are you afraid? "Unidentified UN soldier: Of course. "Reporter 2: Why? "Unidentified UN soldier: I don't know what you're doing for me. "Reporter 2: Are you afraid from the air? From the NATO bombardments? "Unidentified UN soldier: I am afraid. I don't know when will be NATO bombarding. "Reporter: It is the international community and its decisions who have brought the situation upon these people. Whether they are going to survive depends on NATO actions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think interpretation was now [Realtime transcript read in error "not"] provided in English, B/C/S, French and Polish. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, can you identify the person sitting in front of the spherical structure and being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I said that interpretation was provided, I said it was "now provided" rather than "not provided." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, can you identify the person sitting in front of the spherical structure and being interviewed, please.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Of course. It is myself, and a reporter that accompanied us in the car, in the vehicle, that we were transported in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you able to determine if this is the first or second day of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It is the first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And were you told what would happen to you next?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't. When we arrived, before I was handcuffed to the antenna, the reporter gave me something to drink. I asked to be given something to drink because for eight hours I had not eaten anything or drunk anything and I was desperate for water. And the reporter implied that I should not be afraid, that they would just be filming.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 22417B into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22417B receives number P2803, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2803 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This time I'm going to show the witness another videotape and this has 65 ter 22417D. If I can ask Ms. Stewart to start at two minutes into the clip and to pause immediately at the two-minute mark. That's great.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, can you identify the man in camouflage in the image in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, that was a colleague from my team, a Brazilian. We called him Harley. I don't know whether it was his first name or whether it was his last name, but that's how we referred to him. He called me Janusz; I called him Harley.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can ask Ms. Stewart to continue the clip to the end, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We had no problems with the Serb army. I wanted to send a message to my family not to worry, that things are fine. "Q. Were you given food and drink? "A. Yes, both food and drink. We could also wash ourselves. "That is what UNPROFOR members held by the Serbs had to say."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The transcript does not reflect the footage. We tried to follow but it was too quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, you have heard the -- do you rely on the words of the text spoken or --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What's been provided into the record is sufficient for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it is accurate. That was the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My understanding is that is accurate. I don't know if I'm misunderstanding the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the interpreter said it was too quick. Has the Defence listened in?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did listen to the footage but my knowledge of English is insufficient to judge the accuracy. However we have been provided with a transcript of this conversation, and I can't say off the cuff whether it is accurate or not. But we do have the transcript and, last night, we compared the transcript provided by the OTP to what we have, and it is identical to what the witness said. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then everyone is invited to carefully look not only at the interpretation given in court but also to have a look at the transcript provided and I take it attached to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless you would have any very specific questions about the words spoken, I would suggest that we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can you identify the person being interviewed in the -- most of the clip?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, that is myself. And -- for the second time in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the second time"?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Because the first time we saw the first clip and it was the 26th of May. And the second time, I was taken with another colleague, with that Brazilian, and it was on 27, most likely, if I remember correctly. That was on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: To the same place, but the interview was about whether we were given food, whether we were able to wash ourselves, and then I was asked if my life depends on the air-strike. And that was the mystification, that we were handcuffed all the time. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, I heard the word, which is missing at the transcript at this moment, as "mystification." Now, it was not entirely clear what the witness meant in this context by that expression. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yeah. I was trying to figure that out myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, you used a word that didn't come through clearly in the translation. It sounded -- it was in the sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it is in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It is now in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You said something like: "That was the mystification, that were handcuffed all the time." Is that what you said, and if so, what did you mean by it?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: What I meant was that a person who was watching that clip on TV would be under the impression that I was there for 24 hours and that all the time or longer than that I was handcuffed, and it was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 22417D into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22417D receives number P2804, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2804 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My last questions, Mr. Kalbarczyk, deal with after the incident. After your release, did you return to serve as an UNMO in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. I was given a ten-day leave. I returned to my country, and then I was back on my mission. I came back to my sector. And once I returned to the sector, I was deployed in a different sector, and that was the Dubrovnik sector. In the Dubrovnik sector, I was deployed until end of November or beginning of October. I cannot recall the exact -- end of September and the beginning of October. I cannot recall the exact date. And then, from that sector, I was transferred again to the Tuzla sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: How did the experience of being a hostage impact your sense of security as an UNMO for the rest of your time in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, it impacted me fundamentally because I noticed that whenever we were going through the Serb check-points, my body was reacting in a strange way whenever I could see the Serbs. And I never experienced that before. I was nervous and I was anxious. That was my main observation that I could detect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you ever tell your wife and children the details of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: To be quite honest, until this day, I have never spoken about it with my wife or my family. All they knew was what I said to the media and to the press.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell them the details of what happened?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I noticed when I was giving interviews to the press, because the first longer interview I give at -- back at my work, when I was on that leave, when -- after my release. I noticed at that time that it was difficult for me to talk about that, and I noticed that it made me very emotional. I felt like I would cry. I wanted to spare that for my family. And I think that in the near future, after 20 years, it will be a good opportunity to talk about it now when I will be calm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers and your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions. I do have associated exhibits, and I can deal with those now or after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we better deal with it at the very end of the testimony. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine witness? Mr. Kalbarczyk, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify some of your answers provided to my learned friend from the Prosecution with respect to your tasks. Can you tell the Court what was the area you and your team were obliged to monitor?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: At this point, I'm not able to give you a precise description. We had a map, and on that map, it was marked the whole area that we were responsible to supervise. And the points where Serbian troops were deployed were clearly marked on that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... provided precise instruction, in terms of what the obligations of the warring parties were, with respect to honouring the cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: The team leader had such instructions and the team leader would give tasks to each patrol. We had general knowledge regarding our tasks during the -- during patrolling and also during the time when we were at Pale for personal reasons, to get supplies or to take some rest, and to get in touch with local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you obliged while supervising and inspecting check-points held by the VRS to announce your arrival?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. Each patrol was obliged to give a notice of the upcoming visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In case you observed breaches of the cease-fire agreement, were you obliged to put it in writing in your daily reports, in order to inform your sector?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I did not receive translation. [In English] I don't have translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try again. The question, Colonel, was this: In case you observed violations of the cease-fire agreement, were you obliged to inform your sector in writing, in terms of what you had observed?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No. We had to report to the team leader. And if the team leader was absent, then there was a deputy team leader. Or we would report that on the radio to the sector command in Sarajevo. And we were supposed to report any doubts or any comments that we wanted to share.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, 1995, you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina. How many days later did you take up your duties in Pale?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, I was in Zagreb, and I came to Sarajevo two or three days later. Because in Zagreb, we had the first training. We were learning about our area of responsibility, learning about -- about the situation, general situation, in the former Yugoslavia. And, after two or three days, when I was in the Sarajevo sector, there, there was one- or two-day training first and then -- and I didn't know where I would be deployed. Then my deployment was to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you this in order to determine what the time was when you were in Pale. So it was in the second half of April 1995, and you seem to have stayed there until May 26, 1995. During that time, were you able to observe any cease-fire violations by any of the sides, and did you inform your superiors about it?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I was a young observer in this area, nearly a month only. My main task was to participate, to be part of the patrol with a senior colleague who has been there for a longer period of time. And as far as I remember, there were no incidents, important incidents, testifying to any -- or proving violations of the cease-fire agreement between the parties. The relations between the teams of the Serbian check-points, as far as I could have observed, were very good, friendly. Nothing indicated that would change.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I ask you that because, in your statement, you say that some five days before the air-strikes, you had received an order by which your movement was restricted and that it was recommended by your staff, by your headquarters, to adhere to the restriction instructions. Do you know what the reason was to impose such restrictions?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: First of all, this order did not pertain to me personally but to all the teams that were deployed in Pale, and I learned about this from my team leader. I learned that we could not perform our regular duties, that is, patrolling. And -- and the headquarters in Sarajevo confirmed that they -- we should stay where we were housed, where our team was resident, and all we could do, we could only go to do some necessary shopping. We could only buy some food articles that we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the reason made known to you why your headquarters advised you to refrain from any further activity?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Generally the command -- the headquarters do not explain to the soldiers their decisions. We didn't know why. The order was an order and had to be obeyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. And, at the same time, the Chamber noticed that Mr. Mladic would like to consult with counsel. Therefore, let's take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, we'll take a break of 20 minutes, and we'd like to see you back after that. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have any information to the effect that, at the time, there was an ultimatum from NATO directed against the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I did not have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please clarify to us the following. Do you remember if the NATO air-strikes had been in progress for two days before the people you described took you to Jahorinski Potok, or was it -- did it go on only for that one day, according to your memory?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I can say that these air-strikes, which are mentioned, I felt them, and I can confirm they lasted one day. Whether there were any other strikes in any other places, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if you remember, can you tell us where you were on the previous day, the 25th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I was on a three-day rest in Zagreb; and if I remember, I returned in the evening on the 25th of May. It was strange to me that I was the only one on a plane flying to Sarajevo. Usually there were more people. On the 26th, I didn't know what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you landed at Sarajevo airport on the 25th of May, can you give us the precise hour at which you arrived at your premises at Pale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what's the relevance of all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to use a portion of a video-clip which shows that there had been shelling on the 25th as well and there was also a witness to corroborate that. I just want to find out whether it happened before or after the witness's arrival. The first shelling took place on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean the shelling, NATO air-strikes? Or other shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The NATO air-strikes, the first ones, were on the 25th, at the time when, according to the memory of this witness, he arrived in Sarajevo by plane from Zagreb and was transferred to Pale. We want to check whether it was before or after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness told us that he was unaware of any NATO air-strikes on days previous to the one when he noticed it. So ... and, apart from that, even if they would have been there, if there's documentary evidence on that, whether the witness heard it or not, is that -- makes that a difference? Or are you testing the reliability of the witness in this context? Then go directly to the issue, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Case Manager please help me, because I would like to show a section from V000-0515, from the beginning of the video-clip until 2.38. There is also a part which is an introduction in voice-over but -- but we are not interested in that. We just want to show the rest because at this moment we don't have a transcript of that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is it in order to establish that those air-strikes took place, or is it for any other purpose that you want us to look at the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, in order to establish how the air-strikes came about and to describe the atmosphere at Pale at the time when this witness arrived there on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about air-strikes on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can limit ourselves to what then remains the purpose of showing it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now play it until 2:38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we have first patiently looked at one minute of just text which you say you would not rely on. Then we looked at a -- some pictures of the population apparently running, seemed to be in some panic. Is there any dispute about that NATO air-strikes may have -- that NATO air-strikes may have caused the population to start running and being panicking about what happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the third thing I observe is that apparently -- but perhaps we should ask the witness first. When you arrived in Sarajevo on the evening of the 25th, was it still daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was almost dusk. We had to switch on the lights in our car when we were driving towards Pale. But in Sarajevo, it was still sort of -- I mean, it was still daylight but it was almost twilight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Stojanovic, we have seen that at least major portions of the video are in what seems to be full daylight. So, for many, many reasons, there's only a limited relevance for what we played. Now if you want to put questions on the relevant portions, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have any trouble, any problems, or was your movement restricted when you arrived at your headquarters on that afternoon of the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: When I returned to my team, in my vehicle there were people from my team because they wanted to escort me. I learned in the vehicle that our patrolling was restricted. But, on that day, it was quiet. It was eerily quiet. At the check-points, everything was peaceful, calm. Nothing indicated that the next day would be as it was, as you showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now together --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- Witness, the one good reason perhaps for which we looked at someone reporting on television is that it indicates a date. From your answer, I took it that you considered the images to relate to the 26th of May; whereas it appears from the video shown that the television report dates back to the 25th of May. Is there -- the parties do agree that the NATO air-strikes started already on the 25th of May. So, therefore, Witness, if you say, On the day I arrived it was not as it was on the following day, and you suggested that that was shown in the television report, that is then most likely a mistake, because the television report seems to date the 25th. Now is there any chance -- Mr. Mladic is supposed to remain seated, and I'm not going to repeat that again, Mr. Mladic. Either you may not have been present on the 25th of May when air-strikes were conducted, or is there any chance that you may have mixed up that dates that you arrived, for example, on the evening of the 24th, and that you were -- that the events you describe happened on the 25th. Could I ask you to consider that possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am certain that it could not have happened on the 25th. If I had returned on the 24th, I would have said that I was witness to such situations. But this situation reminds of the 26th, in the morning, when, before the main strike into the most sensitive area, that is, ammo depot, there were sirens, the population was running in panic. They wanted to hide. And I cannot say whether these images are from Pale or any other place. But I witnessed similar situations on the 26th, between 8.00 and 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which does not exclude for the possibility that the same happened the day before, when you had not arrived in Pale. Mr. Stojanovic -- Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking, no standing. Otherwise, you will know what the possible consequences are. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we're not talking about the morning hours of the 26th. Let us clarify that part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get P2801 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is your statement. And I would like to see page 2 in both languages, and let us focus on paragraph 4. Colonel, you say -- or, rather, here you speak about the moment when, on the 26th of May, on your premises, around 10.00, you were detained by three men who had entered your premises. But what I like to know, and you have this in front of you, you say that, according to your memory, three men wearing police uniforms arrived. In a car, there was a police official, who may have been 45 to 48 years of age, and two soldiers with Kalashnikovs. The soldiers were also police members because they wore purple uniforms. The first thing I would like you to say, Colonel, is the following: How do you know that this man who was 45 to 48 years of age was, indeed, a police official?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: As far as I could see, their uniforms looked like the uniforms of the police in Pale. And, apart from that, I this seen this very person next to a police building in Pale. He know -- he knew us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the other two men who arrived with him, were they also police members, as you say? You concluded that based on the violet uniforms they were wearing. Is that the only thing that made you conclude that they were police members from Pale?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: In all this stress, I could not even think who these people were. That was the only reason why I thought they were policemen; the colour of the uniform. Well, another reason was what happened next, when an officer entered with some BSA soldiers. And he approached the three policemen, and he said to them that on behalf of the Bosnian Army, of the Srpska army, that he would now take over into his care, that he would arrest us. So it seems that these were no other people than those connected to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would the conclusion be correct that you were at first arrested by police members and subsequently taken over by the army? Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Exactly. However, I should add at this stage that the commander of the police was very surprised, and he was not very willing to -- for the army to take us over. And after some discussion, he relented, and he agreed for us to be taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how and to who that police officer spoke?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: The discussion took place between the police officer and an officer of the BSA. I don't remember whether the police officer made a phone call or anything like that. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you to look at the following page of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, P25801 [as interpreted]. I will -- I need the following page, which is page 3, and that -- I'm interested in the second paragraph in B/C/S and the third one in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph, you describe the first instance when you were taken to that radio relay station on Jahorina mountain. Here's what I'm interested in. In which vehicle were you taken up there to that facility on Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I believe it was the vehicle that they took over. It was, I think, a white Toyota Land Rover.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you and Mr. Rechner were escorted by an officer with a camera, a civilian who was a journalist, the BSA driver, and a masked uniformed soldier. Now, firstly, based on what did you arrive at the conclusion that the man with the camera was an officer? Did he have any military or police insignia?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I don't think I said it was an officer. I just said that he was uniformed, but I am sure that he was the one filming me when I was handcuffed in Jahorinski Potok, before I was moved to the mountain with the antennas. It was the very same person. I just associated him with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you have the third paragraph in front of you. Let us take a look at it together. It says: "After four to five hours, it was about 1630 or 1700, a soldier and policeman came and they took me to the same UN car with Rechner. At that moment, as I was walking to the car, I saw Kozusnik, Teterevsky, the Czech from 7 Lima Team, and Dmitri. They were still handcuffed. I could not see Evans and Romero. I was handcuffed to Rechner and we were put in the car." And then you go on to say: "I did not know where we were going, but it was a road to Sarajevo. In the car, there was the officer with the camera." So your statement shows that you identified him to be an officer.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: In the first statement I indeed said this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I note, Your Honour, if you look at the remainder of that sentence, and this is to be clarified by the witness, it says: "A civilian, I think he was a journalist ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, it's ambiguous language. Whether the civilian depicts a new person then further identified as likely being a journalist or whether the officer, which seems to be a bit contradictory, is described as a civilian. So, therefore, I would have preferred, Mr. Stojanovic, you would have read the whole of the sentence, but your suggestion, Ms. MacGregor, is not one I and perhaps also my colleagues would immediately share.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My suggestion is that he be read the entire sentence and asked to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours. And there will certainly be more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say in your statement: [No interpretation]. "... in the car there was the officer with the camera, a civilian, I think he was a journalist, the BSA driver and a masked uniformed soldier." Here's my question: Was that person with a camera an officer and if you -- if that is what you remember, based on what did you draw the conclusion that he was, indeed, an officer?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Today, after 18 years, I'm not going to resolve whether this particular wording is correct. I think that the statement that I gave was given much earlier, and today I may only say that I most likely associated that person with an officer because I must have seen him at some post that we visited. And, therefore, I thought him to be an officer. Today, I'm not able to resolve whether he was an officer or not. I simply uphold my first statement that was quoted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're unable to say whether that person was a military officer or a police officer.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: The uniform that he was wearing was rather the BSA uniform. Rather -- but rather, for sure it wasn't the uniform of a police officer. Besides, as far as I remember, after these incidents, when we had lunch, he was sitting next to me, and he talked to me like an officer to an officer. I doubted whether it would be admissible for an ordinary soldier to sit next to the officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the basis of your conclusion that the driver was a member of the VRS and not of the police or of some other paramilitary structure?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I might have tell the difference by the uniform only. And I saw two types of uniforms: Police officer would wear like a violet-coloured uniform; and the -- there was also other uniforms that soldiers would wear. But what were the particular units of the soldiers, I cannot tell. However, I may say that, by uniforms, I could differentiate between police officers and members of other units that were operating within that territory; for instance, members of BSA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the four people who were with you and Rechner in the car say anything in English as you were driving?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Only the civilian addressed me in English. And most likely, it was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Neither the civilian nor any other person in the car did say, at any point in time, where you were heading.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: That's correct. We didn't know where we were going. We didn't know why we were blindfolded. That was very stressful. We might have been thinking that they were taking us somewhere to shoot us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the travel, did any of those present in their mutual conversation mention General Mladic in any way?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I have not heard any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, were you able to follow the conversation among the other persons in the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not really, because they were not engaged in any discussion. They didn't talk much; but on top of it, I was not able to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that would be the first question. And you could have left out the second one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Rechner with you in the car throughout?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, he was with me all the time. We were handcuffed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P2554 shown in e-court. Could we focus our attention on page 20, paragraph 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While waiting for it to be uploaded, Colonel, I wanted to tell you that I am about to show you a portion from Mr. Patrick Rechner's statement, where he describes the same event by saying, inter alia, that together with you in that car --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it in B/C/S as well, please. Paragraph 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see it, Colonel, before you. He says: "On the way to the Jahorina radar site, one BSA soldier asked another why we were being transported to Jahorina. The other BSA soldier answered that Mladic had told them he wanted to have several UN members filmed at that location." I'm asking you this: While understanding your previous answers and allowing for the possibility that you may or may not understand the language sufficiently, when you heard this part of Mr. Rechner's statement, I wanted to know whether, at any point in time, you could have gained any insight into the conversation with reference to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I could not. I was focussed on myself, and I did not follow any conversation that unfolded in the car. If my colleague, Patrick, was able to hear that, it means that it might have happened. He was able to understand the Serbian language a little bit. Therefore, I may not rule out that what he said is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: Having arrived close to the radar facility, could you, at any point in time, observe what was happening with Mr. Rechner as you were being taken to the radio relay node where the footage was taken, that part of the footage which we had occasion to see a little while ago?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: When I was taken to the antenna and I was handcuffed to the concrete base, that was the last moment when I could see Rechner standing next to the car, so he was within the field of my vision. After that, when they finished filming, I came back to the car and he was there. I didn't have to wait for him. I was not focussed on observing what he was doing because I was engaged in conversation with that civilian journalist. I presume that he was right on that spot next to the car, but I may not say for sure whether he was talking to anyone or not. After they finished filming, and after they finished that short interview where I just described my situation and the circumstances of other people who were taken as hostages, the filming was completed, and, therefore, our stay in that location came to an end. And the next stage was the return trip on the same road to the building where we were invited for lunch. And this is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the people who were in the car, meaning the civilian journalist and the cameraman, were you in any way mistreated by them? Abused, hit?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No. I would say that it was a nice surprise. Because I asked for some water, since I have not had anything in my mouth for ten hours. And, as I mentioned earlier, it was a very hot day. So I was given some water. And that civilian journalist addressed me in English. He said that I should not be afraid, that there is no threat, that they will be just filming me against the antenna dropout. Because it was important to me. He, in a sense, took my thoughts away from -- no, from thinking about the bad ending of that journey, and I was really grateful to him for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He told us that it was he who told you that there was no reason to fear anything and that immediately following the conversation, you were to be returned to Pale. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It -- there was no conversation to the fact that -- where I would be taken. He simply said that nothing would happen to me at the place where I was taken. But what will be the return journey, where they would take me back, no conversation about that was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, so that I can understand and follow the evidence. When you say, "He told us that he was he who told you that there was" -- who are these "hes" referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The cameraman? Or Rechner?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I apologise for being unclear. In preparation for today's testimony, we spoke to the journalist, and he told us that. I was merely asking the witness whether his recollection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask the question. Ask the witness and use the names in the place of those prepositions for "he" and "he."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution objects to the portion of the statement -- excuse me, the question Mr. Stojanovic just posed about his conversation out of court with the journalist. It's not anything that's in evidence and, at this point, it's testimony from Mr. Stojanovic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think referring to unknown interviews with potential witnesses is not something we would usually do. If you would have simply asked the witness what he said already, by the way, that it was the journalist who told him not to have any fear at that time, then the only thing remaining is that that journalist would have told Mr. Kalbarczyk also that they went back to Pale, which he now says was not said by the journalist. I don't know how important that is, how relevant that is, but I think you should have better refrained from referring to, and in a very unclear way, to an interview you may have had with the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us whether, throughout your stay at the radio-relay facility, was there an entire group that came with you in the car present as well, including the cameraman, the civilian journalist, the driver, and the masked uniformed soldier? Were they, too, present throughout your stay at the facility? Were they close by?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I suppose, yes, they were, although within the field of my vision I could not see all of them. But I learned later that there were some sculpted bunkers with apparatus operating this station, and this is where my colleagues were and the other Pole, who was also a Military Observer. They were hidden in those bunkers, in those shelters. Two observers were outside in the distance of about 20 metres, and they were handcuffed. I don't know what they were handcuffed to. It was some kind of -- something that they were handcuffed to on the earth. They were sitting back to back. I could see those two persons. I didn't see the other persons. Only later did I learn that they were there. So when the filming was over, we did not wait for somebody to -- to leave this place. All of us who came to that place left the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you that for the following reason. If the target had been targeted by NATO aircraft at that particular point in time, is it correct that you would not be the only person hurt but, rather, all of those who were there with you as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, first of all, there's no need to explain why you ask a question. Second, if there is a risk that someone is hit, of course, anyone close to him is at risk to be hit as well. Don't ask for the obvious. I mean -- I have a question. During this second trip, Witness, were you interviewed again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that journey, no. We again were blindfolded, and only when we got to -- well, a kind of a building - they say that was some remnants of the Winter Olympic Games in Sarajevo - the blindfolds were taken off, and we were invited to lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean, when you said that you were blindfolded. You travelled on small roads in the mountains. When you were in the mountains, there were two big radar antennas. Were you then interviewed at that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As was shown in the video, I was only asked to make a statement what had happened and why I was there. So my words were restricted to saying that. I simply said that I was arrested, and if there would be another air-strike to that facility to which I was handcuffed, I would probably be killed. And that's all. The journalist did not need anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're asking the witness whether the camera was with them, the cameraman, whether the journalist was there. We have looked at a video. What's the use of asking? I mean, you can't film someone without having a cameraman there. You can't be interviewed, as we saw on the video, that there's -- as the witness said, there was a journalist who put questions to him. And then it's all for the obvious, that is, that if other people are there as well, that, of course, they are likely to be struck by any air-strike. It's -- let's -- let's be realistic. It's obvious. You could have done it with one question. That is, how many people were there with you, as far as you remember. That would have done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At some point this time, you mentioned bunkers which were close by. They were close to the place where you were filmed. I wanted to ask you what the distance was between you - that is to say, the place where you were filmed - and the bunkers was?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: These bunkers were well masked so you couldn't actually say that there were bunkers. There was some entrance carved in the rock, and I learned this from a colleague when I was released, that they were not some -- some buildings. But when I came, all I saw was antenna. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kalbarczyk, you have not seen the bunkers or the entrance to the bunkers, or have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see the entrance. I learned later that there was an entrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore you cannot tell us at what distance they were from where you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, on the basis on what I learned later. Namely, my colleague said: We were about 20 metres, precisely 20 metres, in the bunker, 20 metres away from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the question was about the distance between you and the bunkers. The question has now been answered. Please proceed. Should we take a break, Mr. Stojanovic. It's time for a break approximately. Could you tell us how much time you would still need, if you would put relevant and non-repetitious questions to the witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 to 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back, Mr. Kalbarczyk, in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to put on the record that the Prosecution prefers to continue with the testimony of Ms. Tabeau on Monday morning and that it is not objected to by the Defence. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber agrees that we would start on Monday morning with the testimony of Ms. Tabeau and would only, after that testimony has been concluded, continue with the next witness on the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, at some point after you had been taken to that radio-relay centre for the second time, according to your memory, on the 28th of May, it was offered to you to leave the Pale area and return to your mission. Can you tell us who it was who made that suggestion to you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: There was no suggestion to leave the Pale area. My colleagues asked me whether I would be willing to be transferred to another area, but it was not because the mission ended, but I was to be accompanied by Russian observers. I did not agree to that. I said that I would remain there where I was. The intermediary was a colleague who spoke English the best, Rechner, and Evans as well, who was deputy team leader at that time. But I was not approached directly from anyone from the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your status while you were at the barracks until the 13th of June? I mean the building where you had accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I'm not sure which building you mean, because, for the first three days, we were in the barracks, and then, after that, we were transferred to a smaller building close to the entrance gate to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That smaller room where you stayed from the 29th of May, 1995, according to your words, did you have -- did you experience any personal harassment, mistreatment, or anything else of the kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Stojanovic, are you interested in an answer to your previous question or not? Because we've only dealt with the room where the witness was in but not what his status was, apart from what you exactly meant by status. If you wanted to ask him whether he considered himself to be a prisoner of war, if that's the issue, then please ask him that question rather than a vague notice of status. But I do not see that the previous question has been answered. Please proceed, as you deem fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My first question would be the following: In those barracks, as you called it, in that facility, did you have -- did you experience any personal harassment or mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Let me answer to your question first. In the barracks, we all felt like we were live shields, and we were told this. We were told that we are in a place from which we can any moment be transported to another location where they believed it would be necessary for us to be handcuffed to an object so that they can shield themselves against any possible air-strikes. Now, as for the -- for your second question, whether I was in any way mistreated or harassed, no. I think it was all very regular treatment for this kind of occurrence, for this kind of incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any official ever tell you that your status was that of a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Nobody informed us what our status was. With time, we felt that those who organised our detainment tried to approximate our treatment to international norms. That is, we were in touch with the Red Cross, with doctors. So it was moving towards this direction. But that happened only after three, four days, during which I believe our status was human shields.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mention -- and let us, again, take a look together at P2801, page 5 in both B/C/S and English, the third paragraph. You mention that, according to your memory, on the 2nd or 3rd of June, General Mladic in civilian clothes visited you in -- in the facility where you were. There were also other persons wearing civilian clothes on that occasion. Let us just wait for it to appear on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us first: At that time, on the 2nd or 3rd of June, which facility were you in?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: In the smaller building near the entrance gate, the gate to the barracks. I believe this was place where guards people were, watch place, as far as my experience tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until then, you had never had the occasion to see General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No direct contact. But I had seen his face from the press, from the television, so I was familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anybody else, any other member of that delegation that visited you then?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, not that I recall. To tell you the truth, I didn't attach much importance to it. I just noticed this one face and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any contacts or conversations between that delegation in civilian clothes and any one of you?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: While the delegation was present, we were obliged to stay in our rooms, and some of us were called to talk to the delegation. As far as I know, later I learned that it was Evans, Captain Evans, as the pilot and Olik [phoen] from Lima 7, as pilot from the Czech Republic. I know about these two. I'm not sure whether Rechner was also interrogated. Later I found out from my colleagues who were talking to that delegation that they were asked whether myself, as an air force officer from Poland, might have guided aircrafts at the targets. They denied, and practically I was not called to talk to that delegation. But this is what I found out from my colleagues. And I also know that I did not participate in the meeting with the delegation, and that delegation was probably under the leadership of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your words correctly, on that occasion, you personally didn't even see General Mladic in person, as a member of that delegation in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, you are wrong. Because I saw the delegation approaching the building. I did not directly participate in the talks with the delegation. However, General Mladic, together with other people who accompanied him, entered the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to focus on what the statement says. You say: "I did not know then it was Mladic, but now that I saw him on TV, I know it was him." Here's my question: At what moment did you come to understand that one of the members of that delegation was General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: At the moment when the delegation was approaching the building. If I had any doubts, they dissipated later because when the soldier takes off his uniform, he looks differently, but the face remained the -- remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no visible reactions to the testimony of the witness. No laughing. No gestures. Otherwise, you'll not be able to follow the testimony any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would just like to consult my client for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If your client will adhere strictly to the conditions - no loud speaking, no gestures visible for anyone else, and no standing - then you have an opportunity to consult with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, just a couple more questions concerning this testimony of yours. How long did the delegation stay on the premises?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I think that it was not longer than 30 minutes. Perhaps 20, up to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is our case that on those two days - the 2nd or 3rd of June - General Mladic cannot have been where you say that he was. Do you allow for the possibility that the man wearing civilian clothes whom you saw on that occasion was not General Mladic, after all?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: No, I would not. But I would not firmly insist whether that was the 2nd or the 3rd. Because I gave the dates with the approximation. So if you're looking for any mistakes here, then look at the dates, because it could be even on the 4th. But I know for a fact that such a situation took place, that we were visited by the delegation which was headed by General Mladic. And what I thought at that time, I thought that they were trying to find a reason to explain to the general public why I was arrested because the charge of guiding the aircrafts that were supposed to do the air -- air-strikes was a very severe charge. So I have to say that it was -- we were lucky that they dropped that charge, and that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're an air force officer. Will you agree with me when I say that for NATO aircraft to carry out their actions, a precondition was the -- to locate the targets and to guide the aircraft to the targets?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Can I skip this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're asking not to be -- not to be obliged to answer the question. No, you have to answer the question. The question being that it is necessary for NATO aircraft to carry out, I take it, air-strikes, Mr. Stojanovic, you were referring to, that you couldn't do that without having located the targets and to be guided to the targets. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
