utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, yes. But the aircraft does not have to be guided. If the location of the target is somehow identified and known, then all the devices that are in the cockpit will take care of the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally aware, directly or indirectly, of the fact that members of the British Army specially trained for such tasks were out there in the field in order to guide NATO aircraft to selected targets in the territory of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I was an observer, a Military Observer. I have already described my job, and it was not my job to think about the tasks given to the British soldiers. I did my job, the one that I was empowered to do, and the one that I was ordered to do. This is sort of second guessing if I were to talk about missions of the British soldiers. I don't have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're -- I'm not calling for speculation. I was really interested in whether you had any knowledge of that because there's a reason why I asked that question. Let me now finish with this topic. Did you, at any point, understand that the mandate of the peacekeeping force in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been changed and that by these air-strikes against one side only, the mandate of the UN forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina had changed?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Later I found out. But until air-strikes, we were doing our tasks following the orders that we received from the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "later I found out," please be more precise. When and from whom did you learn about the change in UNPROFOR's mandate in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Most likely it was at the time when I was transferred to Dubrovnik, because I have never returned to the Sarajevo sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let us now, by way of finishing, take a look at D393.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could have that on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so. Witness, can I ask you whether your knowledge of the change in UNPROFOR's mandate was such that you can tell us what exactly changed in that mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite honest, I have to say that I was not made thoroughly familiar with that because in our mission, the responsibility lines were followed, and we were carrying out orders that were given from the Sector Command to our team leader. So they were taking care of adhering to any changes that might have occurred with the UNPROFOR mandate and the mandate of the Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could -- can we get D393, page 4 in both B/C/S and English. But let us first see page 1 so that the witness knows what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is an inter-office memorandum of the United Nations Peace Forces headquarters in Zagreb dated 30 June 1995. The subject is final reports on the detention of UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let us go to page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in paragraph 4, which reads, inter alia, so the report says: "Several UNMOs confirmed during their interview that the guards were placed at the UNMO accommodation to protect the UNMO from violent reactions from the local population." This is in bold type, the last six words: "... who were looking for revenge after the air-strikes. These measures were ordered by the local BSA commanders." Here's my question: Your experience and the statements that you mentioned at the United Nations headquarters, are they such that -- as to show that there was a risk of retaliation from the local population because of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: This is normal. Particularly conditions were created on the first day of air-strikes when we were taken to a place where we have been handcuffed. For ten minutes we stopped in the main square. The door of the car was opened. We were left by the soldiers, unguarded. Anybody could have approached us and they have could spit at our face. Some people threw small stones at us. And that probably -- I mean, the information about this incident reached our headquarters, our command. And that's -- that's probably why the conclusion was drawn not to allow situations in which observers were not protected against any hostilities. So that's -- that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. This concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to -- to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Considering your last answer, Witness, do I understand you well, that you did not gain the impression that you were guarded against any revenge by the population but that, apart from being used as a human shield, that on your way, for ten minutes, you were exposed to the revenge, rather than be guarded against it?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Precisely saying, Your Honour, the building in which we lived was not guarded, and the -- my last words about what -- how we were guarded during our transportation indicates that somebody did not have really good imagination what could have happened when we were left in the car handcuffed to the seats, and the local population in Pale could have approached the car and could have abscise [as interpreted] us, abuse us, as I said, and could have spat -- spat at us. After ten minutes, probably somebody realised that this is becoming dangerous or perhaps an order was given to take us and transport to us the place which was shown in the video-clip where we were handcuffed to the individual facilities. That's what it looked like. That's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I move to another subject, and that is the delegation that visited you and, as you told us, a delegation which included General Mladic. I first take you to your testimony given today. The question was put to you that, until then - and I understand "then" to be the moment that the delegation arrived - until then, you had never had the occasion to see General Mladic; right? Your answer was --

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I would just like to take you through the whole of it. Your answer was: "No direct contact, but I had seen his press from the television so I was familiar with it."

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether you intended to say that you had seen General Mladic before that delegation arrived on television?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: It is certain that already in Zagreb, when Yugoslavia was mentioned, that figure appeared, in the press, on television, even in Poland. But now I recall that one day, the other day, we were going by some place where many officers were assembled, high-ranking officers were assembled, and from a distance of about 50 metres I saw General Mladic in his characteristic uniform. It was just a moment because we were going by car, passing by -- where was it? Definitely on the side of our sector. That was in Pale. We were probably going from Sarajevo in the direction of Pale. And on that occasion, I did not pay any attention. I simply saw some soldiers. And, later, when, on television I saw General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Let me stop you there because I don't want yet to talk about later. I first want to know how, under what circumstances - that is, on television, or, as you just told us, from a distance - you had observed Mr. Mladic either on television or live. You've told us that. Did you have any other occasion before the delegation arrived to see or watch Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Just as I said earlier, I did see him on television, in the press, a photograph, and I'm recalling now that I saw him when we were passing by -- I don't know what that was but that there was a large group of officers, perhaps they were in session, in a meeting, and I saw him in this characteristic uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: And I made sure that this was General Mladic. I asked my colleague, Is that Mladic? And he said yes. But that was just a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it step by step. When you saw him at a distance in passing by, was it that you recognised Mr. Mladic from having seen him earlier on television and that you then did verify with your colleagues whether it was him?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Precisely, yes. That was kind of press, television, confrontation with a living person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I take you to your statement. In your statement, describing the visit, you said: "We were visited by General Mladic in civilian clothes and other people in civilian clothes." You explained why they wanted to see you. And then you continued by saying: "At that moment, I did not know it was Mladic, but now that I saw him on TV, I know it was him." Therefore, you say at that moment you did not know that it was Mladic. Did you not recognise him from earlier television appearance or from this encounter at a distance when you verified whether it was him?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Well, apparently there is some contradiction but please believe me, we had limited possibilities of observing this delegation when it was entering the building. So when I had a first look at this group of civilians, I did not associate one of the persons as Mladic. Well, because if you take off your uniform, your personality changes immediately. I did not see General Mladic on television or in the press without a cap, without a hat. Only later when I associated the faces that I had seen, one of the faces, when I recalled again on Serbian television, I responded immediately, Well, it was Mladic who was there. So I must have had some -- I must have been prompted with a picture somehow that I recognised General Mladic as a member of that delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then to summarise - please correct me when I'm wrong - when you saw this person in civilian clothes, although you had seen General Mladic before on television and in an encounter at distance, at that moment you recognised the person in civilian clothes not as General Mladic, as you had seen him before, but when, at a later stage, you saw him on television, after you were released, I take it, although you didn't say that specifically, but after the visit of the delegation, it was then that, looking at him at television, you then realised that the person you had seen in civilian clothing had been or must have been General Mladic. Is that a fair summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Because, as I said, when a group of civilians comes, in that group I identified a face that I associated with somebody at the time. But at the time I did not know that that was General Mladic. But 10, 15 minutes after that group left, I was informed by the colleagues, but, at the same time, we had television in our general room, Serbian television, and at that time, on the same day, Serbian television often was showing that person, that figure, so I made sure that that was actually the same face. So after my release that would be too far away. So it was almost within the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I already corrected myself in that respect because you had not said so, but you say, seeing him on television was almost immediately after the visit of the delegation, and it was then that you realised that the person in civilian clothes you had seen was the same as the General Mladic you had seen on television?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With this correction, apart from this correction, was my summary accurate?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. The second summary that you've given is correct, accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm interested if you recall what you have seen at that occasion on television. What was the report on television about?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: I don't recall that report. There was lots of news shown, and we did not understand this Serbian language, so we only were paying attention to the pictures. And in those pictures, we very often saw General Mladic with his soldiers or he was also shown in other situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you watched TV on that occasion, was General Mladic shown in civilian clothes or in uniform, on TV?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Let -- let's make something clear: It wasn't television that was reporting news on -- of that particular day. It was some news of the previous days, and some of the news was about -- with -- with General Mladic. Please do not understand that this television report that I saw spoke about this particular visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't suggest that to you. I just wanted to know if you recall if Mr. Mladic was shown in uniform or in civilian clothes at that point in time when you saw the television report.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, on television, I have never seen General Mladic in civilian clothes. That's probably the reason for my shock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My questions are in a slightly different direction. On two occasions today at page 50, line 11 or 10, and at page 51, line 7, you referred to the fact that the people who were looking at you as you were left in the car with the door open could have spat at you. Do you remember that piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you is: Did anyone spit at you at all?

utterances.speaker: JANUSZ KALBARCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. That was very unpleasant because of the circumstances and then I also noticed that there is something bad about it. I was about to give back, to retaliate but -- with my hand, for example, but I could not because I was handcuffed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, do you have any questions in re-examination; and, if so, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I don't have any questions. I just have the associated exhibits to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this -- Mr. Kalbarczyk, this concludes your testimony, unless the questions by the Bench have triggered any need for further questions by the Defence? Apparently not. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mladic would like to consult with counsel, and since we are at the very end of the testimony, you have an opportunity to do so. Under the usual conditions. No -- no loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. No -- I -- again, I don't want to hear your voice. Whispering is the advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions, apparently. Then, Mr. Kalbarczyk, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, either by the parties or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I take the opportunity to thank the Polish interpreters for their assistance in today's hearing. Ms. MacGregor, associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are four associated exhibits and one table of concordance. If it would be easiest, I will list the four 65 ter numbers for the associated exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we already hear in advance whether there will be any objections at all against the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, Your Honour, but I would like to hear which ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, associated exhibits are on the list, I think. There are only four. No objections. Then you can list them all four in one -- in one turn. We don't have to go through them separately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Number one, 11476; number two, 17443; number three, 18750; and number four, 18751.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, in the same sequence. Number one will be P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2805, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2806, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The third would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2807, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the fourth would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2808, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All four admitted into evidence. The table of concordance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The table of concordance has been assigned 65 ter 29114 and we ask that it be added to the exhibit list and also moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections to it be added to the 65 ter list? Then leave is granted. Also no objection against it being admitted. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 29114 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2809, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2809 is admitted into evidence. Very practically, we would be at a time for a break. We have no further witnesses for today. We would re-start with Ms. Tabeau. I have two decisions, all together five pages, to be read. We can do two things. Either take a break now and that you will hear the decisions after the break, after which most likely we would immediately adjourn for the day, or extend this session slightly so as to read the decisions. If Defence would like to consult with Mr. Mladic, they have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We're aware from informal communication that the Chamber also would like to update on the status of the follow-up exhibits with respect to Witness Bowen. Mr. Jeremy is present and able to do that today if that's how the Court would like to proceed. I note that Mr. Ivetic is here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is it rather technical, isn't it? Yes. Another option would be - and I'm looking at the Defence - that it will be communicated by e-mail, to be copied to the Defence, and then, dependant on the content of it, to have it filed rather than it to be read in court. I leave it to the parties. Most important is that the Chamber finally receives the information and that it is publicly available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm happy to proceed in that way if Mr. Ivetic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And ... I -- I again hear a voice which is too loud. Mr. Stojanovic, how will we proceed? Can I read the decisions and then adjourn or would you first like to have the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was kindly asked to convey to you that due to General's personal needs, we should have a break first and then hear the decisions afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now in view of the reason we could take a very short break of five minutes. We could also take the normal break of 20 minutes. Is there any preference for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible, can we have a 20-minute break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a 20-minutes' break and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00. Mr. Jeremy, if your submissions would be very short, then perhaps it's easier to have them on the record, but I didn't want to extend the session beyond what would be comfortable to everyone. But since we will have a new session anyhow, and if it's not too long, I would invite you to make those submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To start with, I'll deal with some pending issues related to documents which were marked for identification during Witness Butler's testimonies -- testimony. First, concerning P2099, the Chamber would like to hear from the Defence by Monday, the 18th of November, as to whether it maintains its objection as to authenticity. I refer you for that matter to transcript pages 16173, 16177, and 16178. Second, concerning Exhibit P2104, the parties are requested to clarify their position as to which of the document's pages are relevant. They are expected to do so by the same date, that is, the 18th of November. And I refer you in this respect to transcript pages 16210 and 16211. Third, as to P2105, the parties are requested to specify, again, by that same date, whether they agree as to the date featured in that document. I refer you to transcript pages 16219 and 20. Fourth, the Chamber has considered the Defence objections to admission of P2109 and P2129, which were not found persuasive, and decides that P2109 and P2129 are admitted into evidence. Fifth, the Prosecution has informed the Chamber that P2126 is a different version of an intercept which is already in evidence and was requested to specify under which exhibit number that intercept is in evidence. This can be found on transcript pages 16369 to 70. The Prosecution is requested to inform the Chamber accordingly by Monday, the 18th of November. As to D360, and as shown on transcript page 16714, the Chamber invited the parties to tender the original French version and submit further information on the document's provenance. This has not happened to date, and the Chamber instructs the parties to do so by Monday, the 18th of November, 2013. With regard to P2183, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution has uploaded, as requested, a new version consisting of chapter 16 of the SFRY Criminal Code and, as a result, P2183 can now be admitted into evidence. Should the Prosecution intend to rely on other parts of the SFRY Criminal Code, it should specify which ones and request their inclusion in the same exhibit number. I think I should add that P2183 is therefore admitted into evidence. As to P2185, bearing Rule 65 ter number 4377, the Prosecution is requested to upload a revised and shortened version, as it committed itself to doing, restricted to the particular pages it seeks to a rely on by Monday, the 18th of November of this year. I refer you to transcript pages 16846 and 47. Turning to P2189, the Prosecution is requested to confirm whether it agrees with the Defence on the translation issue raised in court and, if so, upload a revised translation by Monday, the 18th of November. The relevant exchanges on this can be found on transcript page 16853. As to P2192, the Prosecution was requested to provide more information on provenance, and this has not been done to date. It is therefore requested to do so by Wednesday, the 20th of November. Lastly, with regard to P2198, the Chamber notes that on the 2nd of October of this year, the Prosecution uploaded into e-court a B/C/S translation with doc ID number R001-3471-BCST, and on the 16th of October, the Defence was asked to confirm whether it agreed with the translation. The Defence has not responded to this request. The translation may be attached to P2198, which is hereby admitted into evidence. In addition to these, the parties are reminded that during Witness Butler's testimony, they agreed to follow up on certain issues related to a number of exhibits; namely, P1968, P1153, P1501, P2137, and D285. To date, the Chamber has not been informed as to any actions taken by the parties in this respect and requests to have an update by Wednesday, the 20th of November. And this concludes the Chamber's observations in relation to these still-pending issues in relation to MFI'd documents in relation to Mr. Butler's testimony. I now turn to delivering the Chamber's decision on the admission into evidence of the expert reports of Witness Richard Butler. By notice of the 25th of January, 2012, the Prosecution served Witness Butler's reports on the Defence. These included the VRS corps command responsibility report, the VRS brigade command responsibility report, and the original and revised Srebrenica military narrative, the analytical addendum to revised Srebrenica military narrative chapter 8, and the VRS Main Staff command responsibility report. On the 20th of February, the Defence objected to their admission, and in a decision of the 19th of October, 2012, the Chamber deferred deciding on admission until Witness Butler's testimony. Witness Butler testified before the Chamber from the 3rd until the 17th of September, 2013. At the conclusion of his testimony, the Prosecution tendered the reports, and the Defence objected to two of them, the Srebrenica narratives, which have, in the meantime, been assigned numbers P2202 and P2203. The Defence noted that the narratives recite witness testimony from the Krstic case and objected to the witness's expertise, claiming that he is merely interpreting documents which encroaches on the role of the Chamber. The submissions can be found at transcript pages 16882 and 883. In response, the Prosecution submitted that the narratives refer to 31 witnesses and of these only 12 were not called to testify or presented as 92 bis or quater witnesses in the present case. Six are Bosnian Muslim civilians who, in their evidence in previous cases, identified persons referred to in the Bratunac Brigade roster; three addressed the 15th of July meeting at the Zvornik Brigade, on which evidence has been introduced in this case by other witnesses; another is a Dutch soldier who testified as to prisoners being transferred from Potocari to the Vuk Karadzic school, which, in this case, is dealt with by another Dutch soldier. The eleventh was in effect a comment by Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans which was introduced in this case through Witness Boering. And the twelfth was a survivor of the Orahovac execution, evidence about which was presented in this case by other Orahovac survivors. These submissions with be found on transcript pages 16883 and 884. As to the objection about the references to testimony from the Krstic case, the Chamber notes that this goes to the weight ultimately to be attributed to the narratives and in this respect finds the Prosecution's submissions linking the impugned testimony with evidence from witnesses presented in this case particularly helpful. Turning to the challenge to the witness's expertise, the Chamber recalls that it has already accepted Witness Butler as an expert in military analysis. His reports display the witness's thorough analysis of documents and testimony he reviewed as well as his observations and conclusions. As noted in the Chamber's previous decision on another military analyst, Richard Philipps, the expertise at issue is engaged in reviewing, identifying, and extracting information from multiple sources, and organising a considerable amount of material in a comprehensive manner. The witness's conclusions do not necessarily provide a definitive answer to the issues relevant to the indictment but merely assist the Chamber in making its determinations on the totality of the evidence. With regard to the narratives, the Chamber notes that P2203 is a revised version of P2202, which, as noted in the former's introduction, follows the same format as the original but includes information gained since the original's publication as a result of the Prosecutor's continuing investigations. Given the significant overlaps between the two versions, and that the revised version appears to include at least the majority of the information set out in the original, having both versions in evidence seems superfluous. The Chamber therefore denies admission of the original version without prejudice. As for the remaining reports, the Chamber considers that, on the whole, they meet the standards of admission under Rules 89(C) and 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Consequently, the reports, including their annexes, which have been given exhibit numbers P2200, P2201, and P2203 up to and including P2210, are admitted into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Jeremy, I left it to you whether you would present your submissions orally or do it through an e-mail. May I take it from your presence that you would like to make the submissions orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honours. It should take five minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. As the Chamber will be aware, you asked for an update in respect to a number of items arising out of Witness Jeremy Bowen's testimony and I can provide that update now. Firstly, in respect to the 92 ter statement and testimony of this witness, P2515 MFI, and P2516 MFI, respectively, Defence and Prosecution have discussed this 92 ter statement and testimony, and while discussions have been partially successful from a Prosecution perspective, Defence stand by two of their objections, as I understand it; namely, that the statement and testimony contain expert or opinion testimony and unreliable hearsay testimony and, therefore, on that basis, they continue to object to the admission of those two documents. Notwithstanding that, we tender them for admission into evidence in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you'd like the Chamber to decide on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do that, in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: As regards the eight associated exhibits for this witness, at the request of the Chamber provisional exhibit numbers have been pre-assigned by Madam Registrar. These were P02568 to P02575. And, as I understand it, Defence have no objections to the admission of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P2568 up to P2575 are admitted into evidence. All public exhibits, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Secondly, as regards further documentation re Witness Fraser's testimony in respect to his knowledge of several incidents of apparent attempted deception by the ABiH side in Sarajevo, the Prosecution continues to search for such documentation and will provide an update to the Chamber by close of business today on whether we -- we've been able to identify that. So far, we have not. Thirdly, as regards the BBC Trust findings and the statistical information about the number of cases brought before the BBC Trust, yesterday, Mr. Ivetic provided me with a detailed proposal regarding this, and the Prosecution is still in the process of reviewing this and it will take a little bit of time and we'll update the Chamber further on this next week. Lastly, the Chamber requested further information from the Defence regarding an UNPROFOR report to General Rose dated the 27th of October, 1994, and that was in respect to an incident involving a sniping of a tram on the 25th of October, 1994. That was at transcript page 18129 to 30. And in particular you asked for evidence of the suggestion that evidence in corroboration by Bosnian officials indicates that the shots came from Bosnian-held territory. Just in connection with this, the Prosecution has been able to locate 65 ter 10505A and that's a report from the BiH Ministry of the Interior relating to this particular incident, and I'd invite the Defence to take a look at that with a view to tendering that document. And if the Defence chooses not to tender it, I think it's likely that the Prosecution will tender that from the bar table. And that concludes my submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I can see, there's nothing which requires an immediate response or an immediate decision. I therefore thank you, Mr. Jeremy, for the updates which you have put on the record. Is there any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on the part of the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day, and since we are not sitting tomorrow, we adjourn until Monday, the 18th of November, at 9.30 in the morning, if I'm not mistaken, in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of November, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
